memoryText: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
These three short commands are among the simplest and most challenging in the Bible.

“Rejoice always.” Joy that does not depend on circumstances is possible because its source is the Lord. Paul is not asking us to feel happy about suffering but to rejoice in God’s presence, promises, and salvation. Even tears and joy can coexist.

“Pray without ceasing.” This does not mean we stay on our knees all day, but that we live in constant awareness of God, turning to him in short prayers throughout the day and setting aside times for deeper prayer. It is a posture of dependence.

“Give thanks in all circumstances.” Not for all circumstances, but in them. We can thank God in the midst of loss because he is with us and working. Gratitude changes our outlook.

“For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.” Many people wonder about God’s will. Here is a clear answer: joy, prayer, and thanksgiving. And it is “in Christ Jesus”: the power to do it comes from him.

When your day becomes anxious, say this verse and take one of these three steps right then.
weekInReview: This week you read the end of 1 Thessalonians, with its call to holy living, the day of the Lord, and short commands to rejoice, pray, and give thanks. Three psalms taught confidence and wonder: Psalm 27, one thing I ask, to dwell in the house of the LORD and gaze upon his beauty; Psalm 138, I give you thanks with my whole heart, and the LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; and Psalm 139, I am fearfully and wonderfully made, search me and lead me in the way everlasting. Second Thessalonians comforted the persecuted, warned against being shaken by claims about the day of the Lord, and called the idle to work. First Timothy began the Pastoral Epistles with sound doctrine, prayer for all people, the one mediator, and the qualifications of overseers and deacons. A doctrinal pause considered church government and officers: elders who shepherd and teach, deacons who serve, and a congregation that follows godly leaders.
reflectionQuestions: Psalm 27 says the one thing David asked for was to dwell in the house of the LORD and gaze on his beauty. What would you say is the one thing you most seek? How could you ask God to make knowing him your deepest desire?
Second Thessalonians says, “The Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.” What threat or fear in your life do you need to entrust to God’s faithfulness?

Paul gives Timothy a list of character qualities for church leaders, mostly about integrity and home life. Which of these do you most want to grow in, whether or not you’re a leader? What is one step?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the call to rejoice, pray, and give thanks.
Tell him what you have to give thanks for in your circumstances.
